newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania's Iliescu down but not yet out.
newsitem.headline: Romania's Iliescu down but not yet out.

text.p: Romanian President Ion Iliescu's hopes of an unbroken run in power from the 1989 fall of communism to the next century have been dealt a blow.

Once heir-apparent to Stalinist dictator Nicolae Ceausescu, Iliescu, 66, must try again in two weeks to convince the electorate his blend of paternalism and cautious reform is the right formula for another four years in office.
The strong showing of his rival Emil Constantinescu and the poor performance of his scandal-ridden Party of Social Democracy seem to have shocked a man used to success.
"Iliescu was visibly marked by the outcome of the vote," said political analyst Dorel Sandor. Iliescu appeared glum and depressed when first exit poll results were announced.

The Moscow-educated functionary, accused of masterminding the ousting and execution of Ceausescu in 1989, a charge he denies, must now summon up the reserves he needs to win the run-off contest on November 17.
Opinion polls are still in his favour but his competitor Constantinescu has the wind behind him.
"For Iliescu, accustomed to thinking that only he and his party are right, such results are like a punch in the nose," said a Western diplomat.
Iliescu portrays his opponents as risk-takers and himself as a guarantor of stability able to avoid the more dramatic economic slide of Bulgaria and ethnic conflicts of Yugoslavia.
"It appears that his (Iliescu's) popularity, based on the model of quiet stagnation, has come to an end," said Sandor.
The opposition argues that Iliescu is trying to cling to power at all costs. It promises quicker reform and says Iliescu has blocked the changes needed to solve Romania's problems.
"I see Iliescu in a very sensitive situation," the diplomat said. "Even if he wins the run-offs, he will be a decorative president without a PDSR majority in parliament to back him."
Opposition leaders say Iliescu is a late and reluctant convert to capitalism, moving awkwardly from communist rhetoric only at the behest of Western governments who have threatened to shun Romania.

But during the election rallies of the past two months, Iliescu made great efforts to persuade his audience he was committed to reform and the privatisation of Romania's still largely state-run economy.
Iliescu's backers say he is a skilful political survivor, loyal to friends, even those tainted by corruption charges, but unforgiving of his enemies. They say he will not give up.
"Yesterday's results might give Iliescu a chance to analyse his mistakes and see how he has relied on incompetent people," the western diplomat said.

Sandor said he did not rule out a defeat for Iliescu in the run-offs, given that Constantinescu will pick up support from other failed candidates, like ex-premier Petre Roman and ethnic Hungarian leader Gyorgy Frunda.
Iliescu and his wife Nina have no children. He rarely appears in public with her, though he said in a recent interview that she was solely responsible for family finances.
